lessons.title: Hiring Your First Cleaning Technicians: Where to Find Them
lessons.body:
When you land more clients than you can handle alone, it's time to hire your first cleaning technicians. In Africa, word-of-mouth is your strongest tool. Start by asking your current clients, family, and friends if they know someone reliable. Post on local WhatsApp groups, Facebook Marketplace, and community notice boards. You can also visit local churches, mosques, or community centersâpeople there often know who is trustworthy and looking for work. Another option is to partner with vocational training centers that teach cleaning or hospitality. They can recommend graduates who already have basic skills.

Be clear about what you need. For a residential cleaner, you want someone who is thorough, honest, and able to follow instructions. For commercial cleaning, they may need to work early mornings or late nights. Write a simple job description: duties, hours, pay, and requirements. For example: "Clean 3-bedroom apartment, 3 times a week, 3 hours per visit, pay 1500 KES per visit. Must have own transport to Kilimani." This helps candidates self-select.

When you find candidates, ask them to come for a trial. Pay them for a 2-hour trial clean at a real client's home (with the client's permission). Watch how they work: do they dust behind objects? Do they greet the client politely? Do they arrive on time? This tells you more than any CV. In Africa, many workers don't have formal resumes, so practical tests are essential.

Start by hiring one or two people. You can expand later. Remember to check referencesâcall their previous employer or ask for a community leader's reference. Avoid hiring friends or family unless you are sure they will respect your authority. Your first hires set the tone for your business, so choose people who share your commitment to quality and honesty.

lessons.title: Screening, Interviewing, and Background Checks
lessons.body:
Screening cleaning staff is critical because they will enter people's homes and offices. In Africa, where formal background checks can be limited, you need to be creative and thorough. Start with a phone interview: ask about their previous cleaning experience, why they left their last job, and what they know about cleaning products. Listen for clear answers and a polite tone. Then invite the best candidates for an in-person interview at a neutral place, like a cafÃ© or your office. Ask situational questions: "What would you do if you broke a client's vase?" or "How do you handle a client who complains about your work?" Their answers reveal their problem-solving skills and honesty.

Background checks: Ask for two referencesâprevious employers or community leaders. Call those references and ask specific questions: Was the person punctual? Did they handle money or valuables? Would you hire them again? If possible, visit their neighborhood and ask around. In many African communities, people know each other, so informal checks can be very effective. You can also ask for a police clearance certificate if the job involves handling expensive items. In Kenya, for example, a Certificate of Good Conduct from the DCI costs about 1,000 KES and takes a few weeks. For smaller jobs, a reference may suffice.

During the interview, watch for red flags: vague answers, blaming previous employers, or reluctance to provide references. Trust your gutâif something feels off, don't hire. Also, verify their identity: ask for a national ID or passport and photocopy it. Keep records of all interviews and reference checks. This protects you if a client makes a complaint later.

Remember, you are building a team you can trust. A bad hire can damage your reputation and cost you clients. So take your time. It's better to keep looking than to hire someone unreliable.

lessons.title: Training New Employees on Cleaning Techniques and Safety
lessons.body:
Training is what turns a new hire into a professional cleaning technician. Even if they have experience, they need to learn your standards and methods. Start with a 1-day orientation. Show them your cleaning kit: microfiber cloths, mops, buckets, all-purpose cleaner, disinfectant, glass cleaner, and a vacuum if you have one. Teach them the correct dilution for chemicalsâfor example, 1 capful of bleach per 5 liters of water for disinfecting. Warn them never to mix bleach and ammonia, as it creates toxic gas.

Demonstrate the right techniques: always work from top to bottom, left to right, and dry to wet. In a bathroom, start with the mirror, then sink, then toilet, then floor. Use color-coded cloths: red for toilets, blue for glass, green for general surfaces. This prevents cross-contamination. For floors, sweep first, then mop with a disinfectant solution. Teach them to check corners, under furniture, and behind doorsâclients notice these details.

Safety is non-negotiable. Provide gloves and masks, especially when using strong chemicals. Show them how to lift heavy buckets by bending their knees, not their back. If they use a ladder, ensure it's stable. Teach them to label all cleaning bottles clearly and store chemicals away from food. In case of a spill, they should know to ventilate the area and use the right absorbent material.

After the orientation, do a supervised clean at a real client's home. You clean alongside them, correcting mistakes gently. Then let them lead while you observe. Give feedback: "You did well on the floors, but remember to wipe the light switches." Repeat this for the first 3-5 jobs. Also, create a simple checklist for each type of clean (e.g., kitchen, bathroom) that they can follow. This ensures consistency. Finally, schedule a refresher training every 3 months to introduce new products or address recurring issues. Good training builds confidence and quality.

lessons.title: Creating Employee Schedules and Assigning Teams
lessons.body:
Scheduling is like solving a puzzle: you have clients, cleaners, and time slots. Start by listing all your recurring jobs: which days, what times, and how long each takes. For example, a 3-bedroom home might take 3 hours, while a small office takes 2 hours. Then list your cleaners and their availability. Some may only work mornings, others evenings. Use a simple spreadsheet or a free app like Google Calendar to map out who goes where.

Assign teams based on skills and compatibility. For residential cleans, one cleaner is often enough. For large offices or post-construction cleans, send a team of 2-3. Pair a fast worker with a detail-oriented one. Avoid pairing people who clashâpersonality matters. If you have a trainee, pair them with an experienced technician for the first few weeks.

Create a weekly schedule and share it every Sunday evening via WhatsApp. Include: client name, address, date, time, tasks, and any special notes (e.g., "client has a dog, be careful"). Ask cleaners to confirm they've seen it. For changes or emergencies, have a backup list of cleaners who can cover. Pay attention to travel time between jobsâif two jobs are far apart, allow 30-60 minutes. In African cities with heavy traffic, add extra buffer.

Rotate unpleasant tasks fairly. No one should always clean toilets. Also, consider client preferences: if a client requests a specific cleaner, try to accommodate. But don't overwork anyoneâlimit to 8 hours per day and 5 days a week. Track hours to avoid overtime disputes. Finally, review schedules monthly. As you gain clients, you may need to hire more staff or adjust shifts. A clear schedule reduces confusion and ensures no client is missed.

lessons.title: Motivating and Retaining Cleaning Staff
lessons.body:
Cleaning is hard, often thankless work. To keep good staff, you must motivate them beyond just a paycheck. Start with fair payâresearch local rates. In Nairobi, a full-time cleaner might earn 15,000-25,000 KES per month. Pay on time, every time. If you delay wages, you lose trust. Offer bonuses for exceptional work: 500 KES for a client compliment, or a percentage of new client referrals. Publicly recognize good performance in your team WhatsApp group. A simple "Great job, Mary! The client loved the kitchen" goes a long way.

Provide opportunities to grow. Train them on new skills like carpet cleaning or window washing, which can lead to higher pay. Promote from within: make your best cleaner a team leader with a small salary increase. Give them responsibilityâlet them manage supplies or train new hires. This makes them feel valued.

Create a supportive culture. Check in on them: "How was your weekend?" Listen to their problems. If they have a family emergency, be flexible with time off. Provide uniforms and quality equipmentâit shows you care about their comfort and safety. Celebrate birthdays with a small cake or airtime. These gestures build loyalty.

Retention also means handling issues quickly. If a client complains, investigate fairly. Don't blame the cleaner without hearing their side. If they make a mistake, coach them, don't fire them immediately. But if they steal or are repeatedly dishonest, let them go. Finally, offer long-term incentives: a end-of-year bonus, or a transport allowance. When staff feel respected and see a future with you, they stay. And low turnover saves you money on hiring and training.

lessons.title: Handling Payroll, Taxes, and Worker Classification
lessons.body:
Paying your staff correctly and legally is essential to avoid fines and disputes. First, decide if your cleaners are employees or independent contractors. In most African countries, if you control when, where, and how they work, they are employees. For example, if you set their schedule and provide equipment, they are employees. If they use their own tools and control their hours, they might be contractors. Misclassifying can lead to penalties. When in doubt, consult a local accountant or labour office.

For employees, you must deduct statutory deductions. In Kenya, this includes NSSF (pension) and NHIF (health insurance). As of 2023, NSSF is 6% of gross salary (up to a limit), and NHIF ranges from 150 to 1,700 KES based on income. You also pay PAYE (income tax) if salary exceeds 24,000 KES per month. You can use free online calculators or apps like iTax to compute. Keep accurate records: name, ID, gross pay, deductions, and net pay. Pay via M-Pesa or bank transfer for a clear record. Issue a payslipâeven a handwritten one.

If you hire contractors, they handle their own taxes. But you still need a written contract stating they are independent. Pay them the agreed amount; they invoice you. No deductions. However, many cleaners prefer employee status for benefits.

Set a paydayâsay, the 5th of each month. If you have fewer than 5 employees, you can still register for PAYE and NSSF. It's not as hard as it sounds. Visit your local KRA office or use their online portal. Alternatively, hire a part-time accountant for 5,000 KES per month to handle payroll. This ensures compliance and frees you to focus on growing the business. Always keep payroll records for at least 5 years in case of audits.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Staffing and Team Management for a Home and Office Cleaning Business in Africa

Your cleaning business will only grow as far as your team can carry it. In most African markets â Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, Kigali, Dar es Salaam, Lusaka â the cleaning sector is labour-intensive, low-margin, and reputation-driven. A client who trusts your brand expects the same standard from every technician you send. That means your staffing system must be deliberate: where you recruit, how you screen, how you train, how you schedule, how you pay, and how you keep good people from walking to a competitor.

This practical reference gives you the operating framework. Treat it as a checklist you can adapt to your city, your currency, and your legal environment.

1. Hiring Your First Cleaning Technicians: Where to Find Them

In African cities, the strongest recruitment channel is referral from people you already trust. A current cleaner who brings in a reliable cousin or neighbour is vouching for them. That social accountability reduces theft risk and no-shows. Pay a small referral bonus (e.g., KES 1,000â2,000 in Kenya, GHS 100â200 in Ghana) only after the new hire completes 60 days.

Other channels: local church and mosque notice boards, community WhatsApp groups, vocational training centres (e.g., NITA-accredited institutions in Kenya, NVTI in Ghana, ITIs in Tanzania), and job boards like BrighterMonday, Jobberman, or Fuzu. Avoid hiring directly off the street without screening â it is the fastest route to client complaints.

2. Screening, Interviewing, and Background Checks

You are sending strangers into people's homes and offices. Screening is non-negotiable.

  • ID verification: National ID, voter's card, or passport. Photocopy and keep on file.
  • Two references: One from a previous employer or landlord, one personal. Call both.
  • Police clearance: In Kenya, a Certificate of Good Conduct from the DCI; in Ghana, a police criminal record check; in Nigeria, a police character certificate. Costs vary but are worth it for office contracts.
  • Practical trial: Pay for a 3-hour paid trial clean at a friendly client's site or your own office. Watch technique, punctuality, and attitude.
  • Structured interview: Ask scenario questions â "A client's child spills juice on a white sofa while you're cleaning. What do you do?"

3. Training New Employees on Cleaning Techniques and Safety

Most new hires have cleaned homes informally but have never been trained on commercial standards, chemical dilution, colour-coded cloths, or client confidentiality. Build a 3-day induction:

  • Day 1: Company rules, uniform, attendance, client etiquette, confidentiality agreement.
  • Day 2: Technique stations â washroom, kitchen, floors, glass, dusting sequence (top to bottom, dry to wet, clean to dirty).
  • Day 3: Chemical safety, PPE, incident reporting, and a supervised clean with sign-off.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Chemical Handling

Never mix bleach (sodium hypochlorite) with ammonia-based or acid-based cleaners â this produces toxic chlorine gas that can cause severe respiratory injury or death. Never store chemicals in unlabelled water or soda bottles; accidental ingestion is a common cause of child poisoning in African households. Always dilute per the manufacturer's label, wear gloves and eye protection, and keep a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for every product on site. In Kenya, the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA, 2007) requires employers to provide PPE and information on chemical hazards.

4. Creating Employee Schedules and Assigning Teams

Cleaning work is route-based. Group clients by geography to cut transport time and cost. Assign teams of two â one senior, one junior â so quality is supervised and no single cleaner is alone in a client's premises (this protects both the client and your employee from false accusations).

Use a simple weekly roster shared on WhatsApp the Friday before. In cities with heavy traffic (Lagos, Nairobi, Accra), schedule office cleans before 7 a.m. or after 6 p.m. to avoid peak-hour delays.

Table 1: Sample Weekly Team Roster (Nairobi context)
Team Technician A (Senior) Technician B (Junior) MonâWed Route ThuâSat Route Transport (KES/day)
Team 1Grace W.Peter M.Westlands officesKilimani homes400
Team 2Mercy A.John K.Industrial AreaSouth B homes450
Team 3Faith N.Daniel O.Karen homesCBD offices500
Team 4Esther M.Brian T.ParklandsLavington450

Source: Adapted from standard route-based scheduling practices in facility services; transport figures based on Nairobi matatu fare ranges (2024).

5. Motivating and Retaining Cleaning Staff

Turnover kills profitability. Every replacement costs you recruitment, training, and lost client trust. In a sector where wages are low, retention comes from dignity, predictability, and growth â not just money.

  • Pay on time, every time. Late pay is the number one reason cleaners quit in African cities.
  • Performance bonus: 5â10% of monthly wage for zero client complaints and full attendance.
  • Growth path: Junior â Senior â Team Leader â Supervisor. Post the ladder publicly.
  • Welfare: Lunch allowance, uniform, gloves, transport top-up, and paid leave.
  • Recognition: "Cleaner of the Month" with a small cash prize and a WhatsApp group announcement.

6. Handling Payroll, Taxes, and Worker Classification

This is where many small cleaning businesses get into legal trouble. You must decide: are your cleaners employees (you control hours, tools, and method) or independent contractors? In most African jurisdictions, if you set the schedule, provide the chemicals, and supervise the work, they are employees â and you owe statutory deductions.

Table 2: Statutory Employer Obligations â Selected African Countries (2024)
Country Pension / Social Security Health / Other Payroll Tax (Employer) Key Regulator
Kenya NSSF: 6% employer + 6% employee (capped) SHIF: 2.75% of gross PAYE on employee; employer not taxed on wage KRA, NSSF, SHA
Ghana SSNIT Tier 1: 13% employer + 5.5% employee Tier 2: 5% employer PAYE on employee GRA, SSNIT, NPRA
Nigeria Pension: 10% employer + 8% employee NHF: 2.5% employer; ITF 1% (if eligible) PAYE on employee FIRS, PenCom, NSITF
Rwanda RSSB Pension: 3% employer + 3% employee Maternity leave fund: 0.3% employer PAYE on employee RRA, RSSB
Tanzania NSSF: 10% employer + 10% employee WCF: 0.5% employer (workers' comp) PAYE on employee TRA, NSSF, WCF

Source: Compiled from official regulator websites â KRA (kra.go.ke), GRA (gra.gov.gh), FIRS (firs.gov.ng), RRA (rra.gov.rw), TRA (tra.go.tz), and respective social security authorities, 2024. Rates change; verify current figures before payroll.

Practical tip: Open a separate payroll bank account. Deduct and remit statutory contributions before paying net wages. Keep records for at least 5 years â tax audits in the region increasingly target SMEs.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Recruit through verified referrals and vocational centres â never off the street.
  2. Verify national ID, two references, and police clearance before first assignment.
  3. Run a paid 3-hour trial clean and score against a written rubric.
  4. Deliver a 3-day induction covering technique, chemicals, safety, and client etiquette.
  5. Assign cleaners in pairs and group clients by geographic route.
  6. Publish the weekly roster every Friday and pay transport allowance upfront.
  7. Pay wages on time; add a performance bonus tied to client satisfaction.
  8. Classify workers correctly and remit NSSF/pension, health, and PAYE on schedule.

Further Reading

  • ILO â Decent Work and the Informal Economy (free report)
  • Kenya Revenue Authority â PAYE Employer Guide
  • Ghana Revenue Authority â PAYE and SSNIT Guide
  • Nigeria FIRS â Pay As You Earn (PAYE) Information
  • ILO â Occupational Safety and Health (chemical safety resources)

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills â Home and Office Cleaning Business course. Always confirm current statutory rates and licensing requirements with your national revenue authority and social security body before implementing payroll.

quiz.q: What is the best first step to find reliable cleaning technicians in Africa?
options: A) Post on international job boards
B) Ask current clients and local community groups
C) Hire from online freelancing platforms
D) Run a radio advertisement
quiz.explanation: Word-of-mouth through clients and community groups is the most effective and trusted method in African contexts.

quiz.q: When screening a cleaning candidate, what is a key red flag?
options: A) They have no formal resume
B) They blame previous employers for all problems
C) They ask about pay and hours
D) They arrive early for the interview
quiz.explanation: Blaming previous employers indicates a lack of accountability and potential attitude problems.

quiz.q: What should you do before hiring a cleaner who will handle valuable items?
options: A) Ask for a police clearance certificate
B) Give them a trial without pay
C) Hire them immediately if they seem nice
D) Skip reference checks to save time
quiz.explanation: A police clearance certificate provides an official background check, which is important for trust.

quiz.q: During training, why should you use color-coded cloths?
options: A) To make the cleaning kit look pretty
B) To prevent cross-contamination between areas
C) To reduce the number of cloths needed
D) To follow international standards only
quiz.explanation: Color-coding (e.g., red for toilets, blue for glass) prevents spreading germs from one surface to another.

quiz.q: What is a safe practice when using cleaning chemicals?
options: A) Mix bleach and ammonia for stronger cleaning
B) Store chemicals near food for convenience
C) Never mix bleach and ammonia
D) Use chemicals without gloves to save money
quiz.explanation: Mixing bleach and ammonia creates toxic chloramine gas, which can be fatal.

quiz.q: How often should you schedule refresher training for cleaning staff?
options: A) Every week
B) Every 3 months
C) Once a year
D) Only when a client complains
quiz.explanation: Quarterly refresher training helps reinforce skills and introduce new methods or products.

quiz.q: When creating employee schedules, what should you consider to avoid burnout?
options: A) Assign the same person to all toilet cleaning
B) Limit work to 8 hours per day and 5 days a week
C) Give no breaks between jobs
D) Ignore travel time between clients
quiz.explanation: Limiting hours prevents exhaustion and maintains quality and morale.

quiz.q: What is a good way to share the weekly schedule with your team?
options: A) Post it on a public notice board
B) Send it via WhatsApp every Sunday evening
C) Tell each person verbally on the day
D) Mail a printed copy to their home
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp is widely used in Africa and allows quick confirmation and easy updates.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate unpleasant tasks among team members?
options: A) To ensure fairness and prevent resentment
B) To save money on cleaning supplies
C) To make clients happy
D) To reduce the need for training
quiz.explanation: Fair rotation keeps morale high and prevents staff from feeling exploited.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to motivate cleaning staff without a big budget?
options: A) Give them a company car
B) Publicly recognize good performance in a team chat
C) Increase their hours without extra pay
D) Ignore their personal problems
quiz.explanation: Public recognition is free, boosts morale, and reinforces good work.

quiz.q: What should you do if a client complains about a cleaner?
options: A) Fire the cleaner immediately
B) Investigate fairly and hear the cleaner's side
C) Ignore the complaint
D) Blame the client
quiz.explanation: A fair investigation ensures justice and maintains trust with both client and employee.

quiz.q: How can you retain good cleaning staff?
options: A) Pay them late but give bonuses
B) Offer opportunities to grow and learn new skills
C) Treat them as replaceable
D) Avoid giving any feedback
quiz.explanation: Growth opportunities make staff feel valued and encourage them to stay long-term.

quiz.q: In Kenya, what does NSSF stand for?
options: A) National Social Security Fund
B) National Salary Support Fund
C) National Staff Savings Fund
D) National Security Service Fund
quiz.explanation: NSSF is the National Social Security Fund, a mandatory pension deduction for employees.

quiz.q: When is a cleaning worker considered an independent contractor?
options: A) When you control their schedule and provide tools
B) When they use their own tools and control their hours
C) When they work full-time for you
D) When you pay them a monthly salary
quiz.explanation: Independent contractors have more control over how and when they work, and use their own equipment.

quiz.q: What is a best practice for payroll records?
options: A) Keep them for 6 months
B) Keep them for at least 5 years
C) Discard them after payment
D) Only keep electronic records
quiz.explanation: Keeping records for at least 5 years ensures compliance with tax audits and labour laws.

quiz.q: What is a good way to pay employees to maintain clear records?
options: A) Cash only
B) M-Pesa or bank transfer
C) Cheque
D) Promissory notes
quiz.explanation: Mobile money or bank transfers provide a digital trail, reducing disputes and easing record-keeping.

quiz.q: What should you include in a job description for a cleaning technician?
options: A) Only the pay rate
B) Duties, hours, pay, and requirements
C) The client's name and address
D) Your personal phone number
quiz.explanation: A clear job description helps candidates understand expectations and self-select.

quiz.q: Why is a practical trial important when hiring a cleaner?
options: A) It tests their ability to follow instructions and work quality
B) It saves money on wages
C) It replaces the need for references
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: A paid trial shows real skills, punctuality, and attitude, which are more reliable than a CV.

quiz.q: What is a safe lifting technique for cleaning staff?
options: A) Bend at the waist
B) Bend at the knees and keep back straight
C) Lift with one hand
D) Twist while lifting
quiz.explanation: Bending knees and keeping the back straight prevents back injuries.

quiz.q: What should you do if a cleaner breaks a client's vase?
options: A) Ignore it and hope the client doesn't notice
B) Blame the client for placing it poorly
C) Apologize, replace or compensate, and coach the cleaner
D) Fire the cleaner immediately
quiz.explanation: Taking responsibility and coaching the cleaner maintains trust and improves future performance.

quiz.q: How can you show appreciation to cleaning staff on a low budget?
options: A) Give them a day off without pay
B) Celebrate birthdays with a small cake or airtime
C) Buy them expensive gifts
D) Ignore their birthdays
quiz.explanation: Small, thoughtful gestures like cake or airtime show you care without breaking the bank.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of promoting from within your cleaning team?
options: A) It reduces the need for training
B) It motivates staff and saves on hiring costs
C) It guarantees loyalty forever
D) It allows you to pay less
quiz.explanation: Promotion motivates existing staff and reduces recruitment and onboarding expenses.

quiz.q: What should you do before assigning a team to a large office clean?
options: A) Pair a fast worker with a detail-oriented one
B) Send only one person to save money
C) Ignore their compatibility
D) Assign randomly
quiz.explanation: Balancing speed and detail ensures the job is done thoroughly and efficiently.

quiz.q: Why is it important to confirm that cleaners have seen the weekly schedule?
options: A) To avoid missed appointments and confusion
B) To test their memory
C) To make them feel micro-managed
D) To reduce your phone bill
quiz.explanation: Confirmation ensures everyone knows where to be, preventing no-shows and client dissatisfaction.

quiz.q: What is a statutory deduction in Kenya for employees?
options: A) NHIF
B) Netflix subscription
C) Lunch money
D) Transport allowance
quiz.explanation: NHIF (National Hospital Insurance Fund) is a mandatory health insurance deduction.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are unsure whether a worker is an employee or contractor?
options: A) Guess and hope for the best
B) Consult a local accountant or labour office
C) Treat them as a contractor to avoid taxes
D) Ask the worker to decide
quiz.explanation: Professional advice prevents misclassification penalties and ensures legal compliance.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for paying contractors?
options: A) Deduct NSSF and NHIF
B) Have a written contract and pay against an invoice
C) Pay cash without records
D) Treat them like employees
quiz.explanation: A written contract and invoice clarify the independent relationship and simplify tax handling.

quiz.q: What should you do if a cleaner consistently arrives late?
options: A) Ignore it to keep the peace
B) Have a private conversation and set clear expectations
C) Fire them immediately
D) Reduce their pay without discussion
quiz.explanation: Addressing lateness directly and professionally gives the employee a chance to improve.

quiz.q: Why is it important to provide gloves and masks to cleaning staff?
options: A) To protect them from chemicals and germs
B) To make them look professional
C) To comply with fashion trends
D) To reduce the need for training
quiz.explanation: Gloves and masks protect workers from hazardous chemicals and infectious materials.

quiz.q: What is a key element of a supportive team culture?
options: A) Checking in on employees' well-being
B) Never speaking to them outside work
C) Ignoring personal emergencies
D) Publicly criticizing mistakes
quiz.explanation: Showing genuine care for employees' well-being builds loyalty and a positive work environment.
